body.text: The big ticket question confronting the Quad, however, is how Donald Trump engages with the group and the broader Indo-Pacific geography

Speaking to the media on the sidelines of the G20 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in Atlanta, the U.S. Secretary of State announced that the leaders of the four Quad countries — India, Australia, Japan and the U.S. — are expected to meet in Manila in November, on the sidelines of the ASEAN Summit. The announcement is significant as this would be the first summit-level meeting of the Quad leaders since Donald Trump began his second term as U.S. President. It would also be the first such summit attended by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi since she assumed office. The last Quad Leaders’ Summit was held in Wilmington in 2024, when Joe Biden was U.S. President and Fumio Kishida was Japan’s Prime Minister.

While India was expected to host the subsequent Quad Leaders’ Summit, the grouping underwent a period of intense strategic turbulence in 2025, on account of Washington’s shifting geopolitical priorities and changing political dynamics in its bilateral relations with Quad members, especially India. However, this did not result in complete collapse of the grouping. Apart from the leader-level summit, the group has remained successful in continuing its operational synergies in its various initiatives. This was most evident in the elevation of the Quad’s Indo-Pacific Maritime Domain Awareness initiative to the Indo-Pacific Maritime Surveillance Collaboration framework, launched in New Delhi in May 2026, following the Quad Foreign Ministers’ Meeting.

Additionally, the foreign ministers of the four Quad countries held multiple meetings across 2025 and 2026, a period characterised as the nadir of the group’s political alignment. In 2025, the foreign ministers met twice in Washington, with the first meeting marking Marco Rubio’s first engagement as U.S. Secretary of State. In 2026, they met three times, in New Delhi, Manila, and Atlanta. A natural priority area for the agenda of these meetings was to schedule a leader-level summit for the group. For a grouping of this nature, which has neither a permanent bureaucracy nor an institutional framework of its own, such summits serve as crucial platforms to reaffirm its shared purpose and chart its agenda for the months ahead.

The big ticket question confronting the Quad, however, is how President Trump engages with the group and the broader Indo-Pacific geography. This, in many ways, is going to be the first occasion where Mr. Trump could articulate his vision and outlook towards the region for the remainder of this term. It was during his first tenure in the White House that the Quad was revived in 2017, and the Quad bolstered its approach towards the Indo-Pacific by renaming the U.S. Pacific Command to U.S. Indo-Pacific Command. However, since beginning his second term, Mr. Trump’s priorities have been dictated by the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war, Washington’s approach towards the transatlantic relationship and NATO, and the war in West Asia. Although the U.S. has not publicly expressed disinterest in the Indo-Pacific, regional partners have remained cautious about the possibility of a fundamental shift in Washington’s engagement with the region.

President Trump’s insistence that the U.S. expects its partners to enhance burden-sharing within the transatlantic security architecture it is invested in has also caused concern in the Indo-Pacific. The U.S. continues to remain a significant security actor in the region, especially in the Pacific, with several like-minded countries embedded in the U.S.-led security architecture. Furthermore, the White House’s decision to review AUKUS has heightened concern and uncertainty among other players in the Indo-Pacific. This has prompted various countries to undertake measures to diversify their security policies.

For example, Japan, through its One Cooperative Effort Among Nations (OCEAN) framework, has sought to increasingly reshape its post-war security posture by deepening strategic alignment with partner countries. Australia has made efforts to strengthen defence partnerships with India, Japan, Southeast Asian countries, and Pacific Island countries to deter China’s growing footprint in the region. India continues to pursue a policy of multi-alignment and diversification of defence and strategic ties with like-minded countries in the Indian Ocean and the wider Indo-Pacific.

The recent meeting between the Defence Ministers of JAI (Japan-Australia-India) in Cenu also signals a willingness among these countries to further deepen their partnership notwithstanding the nature and character of Washington’s role in the region. New entrants in the Indo-Pacific strategic landscape, such as France, have also sought to bolster ties with regional countries to sustain a balanced security environment in the region. Even though Mr. Trump’s actions have spurred a rethink on the changing security order in the Indo-Pacific among regional partners, Washington’s role remains critical, especially in the face of a worsening maritime security environment prompted by continued expansion of China’s footprint. Washington’s role in safeguarding the Taiwan Strait, a critical flashpoint in the Indo-Pacific strategic geography, remains significant.

While questions remain about the nature and character of U.S. involvement in the Indo-Pacific, at least for the remainder of President Trump’s tenure in White House, the announcement of the imminent leader-level summit of the Quad appears to have breathed new life into the group. Even though India was expected to host the next leader-level summit following the previous meeting in Wilmington in 2024, the Philippines’ hosting of the summit also reinforces one of the group’s foundational strategic pillars — ASEAN centrality. Arguably, the Philippines remains at the front and centre of Chinese misadventures in the Indo-Pacific, with ongoing tussles over sovereignty issues between Manila and Beijing.

Following the Quad’s track record at previous leader-level summits, its leaders are expected to reiterate the importance of respecting sovereignty in the South and East China Seas and condemn attempts by powers to disregard international law in the region. Delivering such a message from Manila would carry the weight of strategic symbolism. For Mr. Trump, the objectives of this Indo-Pacific visit should be dictated by two priorities: resetting American posture in the region and helping assert the Quad’s commitment against Chinese belligerence from Manila.
This commentary originally appeared in The Hindu.
